opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an important question, because the headline numbers can be misleading if you don't think about what they actually measure.

When we've looked at algorithmic progress in language models, the basic approach is to ask: how much less compute do you need today to reach the same level of performance, say the same perplexity on some held-out text, as you did a few years ago? By that measure, progress has been very fast. The compute needed to reach a fixed loss has been halving roughly every eight months or so, which is faster than Moore's law and faster than what we see in a lot of other areas of computer science.

But there are a couple of caveats I'd emphasize. First, perplexity or loss is a proxy. It correlates with downstream capabilities, but it's not obvious that a given reduction in loss translates into the same amount of progress on the things we actually care about for AGI: long-horizon planning, reliably doing agentic tasks, adapting to new situations, doing the messy work people actually get paid for. You can get big efficiency gains on predicting text without necessarily getting proportional gains on those harder capabilities.

Second, a lot of what we measure as software progress isn't independent of compute. Many algorithmic innovations only pay off at large scale, and they're discovered because labs have access to more compute for experiments. So it's not as if software is a separate engine racing ahead; it's quite entangled with hardware scaling. That matters if you're asking whether software progress alone could carry us to AGI, for example through some kind of intelligence explosion where AI systems improve their own algorithms. If the innovations depend on lots of experimental compute, that loop is more constrained than it first looks.

Third, there's a question of whether the low-hanging fruit is being picked. Fast progress in a young field is common, and it doesn't tell you much about how far the current paradigm can go or whether returns will hold up.

So my overall take is that the rate of software progress is real and impressive, and it's a meaningful part of why AI capabilities have advanced so quickly. But I'd be cautious about reading it as a direct speedometer for progress toward AGI. To assess that, you really want to look at how well these systems perform on economically relevant, general tasks, and at whether they can substitute for human labor across a broad range of jobs. That's ultimately the test that matters, and on that front I think we're still some distance away, even though the trend is clearly moving in that direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to be careful about what you mean by "software progress" here, because a lot of what people point to is progress on benchmarks, and benchmarks are a pretty noisy signal for the thing we actually care about.

So the way I think about it is roughly this. There's a notion of effective compute, where you decompose capability gains into how much physical compute you're throwing at the problem and how much algorithmic efficiency you've gained on top of that. And if you look at the algorithmic side, the estimates we've done suggest something like a doubling of effective compute every eight months or so from algorithmic improvements alone, maybe with fairly wide error bars. That's fast. That's comparable to or faster than the hardware trend. So in that narrow sense, yes, software progress is very rapid.

But the question of whether that's progress toward AGI is a different question, and I think the honest answer is that we don't have a great way to measure it. The benchmarks that models are saturating are mostly benchmarks that were designed because they were things we could write down and grade. They're short-horizon tasks, well-specified, with a clear right answer. And the things that would make a system actually general, in the sense of being able to substitute for a human worker across a wide range of economically valuable tasks, are precisely the things that are hard to put in a benchmark. Long-horizon agency, dealing with messy and underspecified situations, learning on the job, accumulating context over weeks or months. We don't really have good evals for those, and when people try to build them, the models tend to look much weaker than the headline benchmark numbers suggest.

So you get this gap where the models are superhuman on certain exams and still can't reliably do a lot of fairly mundane work. And I think that gap is informative. It tells you that the rate of progress on the measured stuff is an upper bound on the rate of progress on the unmeasured stuff, not a proxy for it.

The other thing I'd flag is that a lot of the recent gains have been from the post-training side, from reinforcement learning on verifiable domains like math and code. That's genuinely impressive, but it's also somewhat domain-specific in a way that pretraining scaling wasn't. It's less clear to me that you can just keep turning that crank and have the capability generalize to tasks where there's no verifier. Maybe you can. But I'd want to see evidence of that rather than assume it.

So my overall assessment is something like: software progress is real and fast, it's clearly moving us in the direction of more capable systems, but I'd put less weight on it as a signal of imminent AGI than a lot of people in the field do. I'd want to see the economic indicators move, actual revenue, actual labor substitution, before I updated hard. And those have been moving, but much more slowly than the benchmark numbers would lead you to expect.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between getting better at language modeling and getting closer to systems that can do the full range of things humans can do. They're related, but they're not the same thing.

For example, you might find an algorithmic improvement that lets you achieve the same language-modeling performance with half as much compute. That's real progress. But translating that into a shorter timeline to AGI requires knowing what capabilities you get as you improve language modeling, and whether the current approach is missing something important.

I'd look at whether the improvements transfer to a broad range of tasks, particularly tasks that weren't specifically targeted during development. Can the models learn unfamiliar things? Can they carry out longer tasks reliably? Do they need less human intervention? Those are more informative than a benchmark score alone.

So the fast rate of software progress is evidence that we should take rapid capability growth seriously. But I wouldn't assume that a given rate of improvement in language modeling translates directly into the same rate of progress toward AGI. That's an additional claim, and there's substantial uncertainty around it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence of progress toward AGI, but it’s difficult to say how much evidence without looking at what’s driving the improvements. You can get better performance by using more compute, by making algorithms more efficient, or by making a system better at a particular task. Those have different implications for what we should expect next.

For example, if an algorithmic improvement lets you achieve the same performance with a tenth of the compute, that’s quite significant. But you can’t necessarily interpret it as moving ten times closer to AGI. It might be an improvement that applies broadly, or it might exploit something specific to the benchmarks we’re measuring.

So I would look at whether the improvements transfer across tasks, whether they continue as we scale, and whether they address the things current systems struggle with. Can they learn unfamiliar tasks? Can they carry out longer projects reliably? Rapid progress in language modeling should update us toward taking shorter timelines seriously, but translating that progress into a date for AGI requires additional assumptions.
